list.listitem: Attempt to identify the cause of nausea and vomiting and provide targeted therapy (see ). C
For patients with persistent or severe symptoms, order a CBC, basic metabolic profile, and pregnancy test (for adolescent and adult patients at risk for pregnancy). C
Evaluate for complications of nausea and vomiting including volume depletion, malnutrition, electrolyte imbalance, and vitamin deficiencies. Treat these appropriately. C

Prevent post-operative nausea with use of dexamethasone, dexmedetomidine, midazolam, droperidol, ondansetron, palonosetron, aprepitant, or gabapentin; combinations of medications appear most effective. B
For prevention of chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting, consider ondansetron, granisetron and various combinations of palonosetron, dexamethasone, aprepitant, and olanzapine. B
Suppress nausea and vomiting if possible with antiemetics A or alternative treatments such as ginger or acupressure; B ultimately, treat the underlying cause when possible. C

background.definition: Nausea is entirely subjective and commonly described as the sensation that immediately precedes vomiting. Vomiting is a highly specific physical event that results in the rapid, forceful evacuation of gastric contents in retrograde fashion from the stomach up to and out of the mouth.

list.listitem: Among pregnant women in 1 study, nausea was reported by 74% and vomiting by 51%. The mean gestational age of onset was 6 weeks and nausea lasted a mean of 35 days (range 1-114), lasted all day long (vs. morning only) in 80%, and took until 22 weeks to resolve in 90% of women.
Overall, 70% to 80% of cancer patients on chemotherapy experience nausea and/or vomiting.

Coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) causes nausea and/or vomiting in 7.8% (95% CI 7.1% to 8.5%) to 9.0% (95% CI 5.5% to 12.9%) of patients based on two meta-analyses. Most studies in the first paper were on hospitalized patients and studies in the second paper were noted to have high risk of bias. Other GI symptoms reported in patients with COVID-19 include diarrhea in 12.4% and 7.7%, and abdominal pain in 2.7% to 6.2%, respectively.
Incidence of postoperative nausea and vomiting (PONV) is 30% in the general population, but can run as high as 70% when including high-risk populations.

The incidence of post-discharge nausea and vomiting from US ambulatory surgery centers was 37% in a prospective multicenter study of 2,170 adults undergoing general anesthesia. Associated factors based on logistic regression analysis were female gender (adjusted OR 1.5), age <50 years (aOR 2.2), history of nausea and/or vomiting after previous anesthesia (aOR 1.5), opioid administration in the postanesthesia care unit (aOR 1.9), and nausea in the postanesthesia care unit (aOR 3.1).
In a small study of 205 children, the overall post-discharge NV incidence was 14.6% (30 of 205); nine suffered from vomiting.

In a retrospective survey study of 12,433 patients undergoing 1 of 5 common ambulatory cancer procedures (prostatectomy, nephrectomy, mastectomy, hysterectomy, or thyroidectomy) at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center from September 2016 to June 2022, nausea was experienced on multiple days by 1485 of 9,300 patients (16%). Vomiting was uncommon, occurring in 139 of 10,812 (1%).
The U.S. prevalence of cyclic vomiting syndrome (CVS) is approximately 2%. CVS is more common in women.

In 2021, vomiting was the ninth highest cause of emergency department visits in the United States. Of recorded ED visits, 2810 out of 139,781 (2%) were for vomiting. Nausea was 12th on the list of reasons for visit with 1804 emergency room visits out of 119,191 recorded in 2006.
Approximately half of people with CVS visit the emergency department annually and 1 in 3 adults with CVS become disabled.
May represent a basic, physiologic homeostatic response to an ingested exogenous toxin or may be indicative of a disease process of the GI tract, adjacent organs, or CNS.
The risk ratio of post-operative nausea and vomiting (PONV) increases by 20% per hour following use of nitrous oxide in the anesthesia gas mixture after 45 minutes of exposure.
Among patients with advanced cancer, nausea and vomiting is related to both treatment (chemotherapy, radiation, surgery) and non-treatment clinical issues related to the cancer.
Vomiting is a reflex behavior controlled and coordinated by a vomiting center in the medulla oblongata. Receptors in various areas of the body provide afferent input to the vomiting center.
Chemicals called emetics can illicit vomiting by stimulating receptors in the stomach, duodenum, or chemoreceptor trigger zone located in the floor of the fourth ventricle.

In diabetic animal models of gastroparesis, investigators found immune dysregulation and injury to the interstitial cells of Cajal and other components of the enteric nervous system through paracrine and oxidative stress mediators.
A hormone derived from the feto-placental unit acting on the brainstem (GDF15) is positively associated with nausea, vomiting and hyperemesis in pregnancy.

In severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2), the host receptor angiotensin-converting enzyme 2, which acts as a infection gateway, is highly expressed in gastrointestinal epithelium and may be responsible for the development of nausea/vomiting that can precede respiratory symptoms.
Scopolamine and antihistamines are useful in preventing motion sickness and its associated nausea.B
Drugs found effective for prevention of PONV include dexamethasone, dexmedetomidine, midazolam, droperidol, ondansetron, palonosetron, aprepitant, gabapentin, and combinations as noted below. B

For prevention of chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting, 2023 evidence-based guidelines are available from the Multinational Association of Supportive Care in Cancer and the European Society for Medical Oncology. The recommendations are summarized below based on emetic potential of the chemotherapy agent and route of administration. A

Scopolamine is more effective than placebo and similar to antihistamines in preventing motion sickness (and its associated nausea). The authors identified no randomized trials examining the effectiveness of scopolamine in the treatment of established motion sickness.

Authors of a metaanalysis of 60 RCTs found that intravenous (IV) dexamethasone 4 to 5 mg or 8 to 10 mg was better than placebo in reducing PONV (NNT 3.7 and 3.8, respectively); the higher doses were not better than lower doses. Dexamethasone 8 mg given 1 hour before total abdominal hysterectomy was somewhat helpful for reducing emesis episodes at hours 2 and 4 after the surgery, but not in hours 0, 6, 12 and 24. Reduced nausea severity was shown with dexamethasone based on an RCT with 102 patients.

Perioperative dexmedetomidine, a selective alpha2-adrenergic agonist with sedative properties, was more effective than placebo in reducing PONV in a meta-analysis of 15 RCTs of patients undergoing laparoscopy. The drug, however, lowered heart rate and mean arterial pressure.

Perioperative midazolam decreases the incidence of PONV over placebo based on two meta-analyses. In an RCT of 120 patients undergoing laparoscopic surgery, midazolam was similar to combination dexamethasone-ondansetron in preventing PONV which occurred in 33.3% and 30%, respectively.
Preoperative gabapentin reduced PONV in 8 trials with PONV as an endpoint, and in 5 trials of bariatric surgery (risk ratio of nausea/vomiting 0.49 at postoperative 6-24 hours).

In an RCT of 574 patients, a single 0.075 mg IV dose of palonosetron (a 5-HT3 receptor antagonist [RA], administered immediately prior to induction of anesthesia) significantly decreased emetic episodes and use of rescue medication in postoperative patients.
A neurokinin 1 receptor antagonist (NK1-RA), rolapitant, was better than placebo in reducing PONV in a dose-dependent manner but was not significantly better than odansetron.

Use of opioid-free anesthetic strategies may also reduce PONV. In a systematic review and meta-analysis of 1934 patients from 26 RCTs, opioid-free anesthesia significantly reduced adverse postoperative events (OR 0.32, 95% CI 0.22 to 0.46, I2 = 56%), primarily through decreased nausea (OR 0.27) and vomiting (OR 0.22). Opioid-free compared to opioid-based anesthesia was also shown to reduce PONV and post-operative complications without clinically significant differences in postoperative pain or opioid consumption based on four meta-analyses. However, there was no difference in PONV between opioid-free and opioid-containing general anesthesia (incidence 10.5% vs. 8.1%, respectively), in an RCT of 152 adult women undergoing elective inpatient gynecological laparoscopy.

Opioid prescribing at surgical discharge does not reduce pain intensity, but increases adverse events including vomiting (RR 4.5, 95% CI 1.9 to 10.5), nausea, constipation, dizziness, and drowsiness based on a systematic review and meta-analysis of 47 trials including 6607 patients (high-to-moderate certainty although trials were rated as low-quality).

In a study of 4,086 surgical patients with a history of PONV, use of several antiemetics concurrently was more effective in reduction of PONV than use of individual agents. Reduction of PONV was greatest when all 3 agents were used (4 mg ondansetron, 4 mg dexamethasone, and 1.25 mg droperidol).

In an RCT of 140 women undergoing ambulatory gynecologic or plastic surgery with general anesthesia, preoperative olanzapine 10 mg, an atypical antipsychotic, in addition to standard antiemetic prophylaxis with dexamethasone and ondansetron vs. standard antiemetic only reduced nausea and/or vomiting in the 24 hours after discharge (14% vs. 38%, respectively; RR 0.37, 95% CI 0.20 to 0.72) and severe nausea (6% vs. 20%; RR 0.28, 95% CI 0.10 to 0.80).

In a PONV-prevention phase III RCT among women, there was a significantly higher complete response rate in the group randomized to ondansetron plus the NK1-RA casopitant mesylate than for those randomized to single dose ondansetron alone at 24 hours (68.7% vs. 58.7% in the ondansetron-only group) but no difference at 24 to 48 hours. Vomiting within 24 hours was also significantly lower in the combination group (10.3% vs. 25.1% of the ondansetron-only group).
The NK1-RA aprepitant is FDA-approved for use in combination with other antiemetic agents for prevention of nausea and vomiting following chemotherapy and for PONV.
A meta-analysis of 10 studies with 1,729 patients suggested that increased intraoperative supplemental oxygen has no effect on overall PONV, regardless of type of surgery.

Among patients on postoperative fentanyl-based IV patient-controlled analgesia (PCA), combination ondansetron and dexamethasone was no better than ondansetron alone in reducing the 48-hour incidence of PONV, although severity appeared less with combination therapy. In a recent RCT including 87 patients undergoing microvascular decompression, ketorolac-based PCA resulted in a decrease in PONV incidence (48.8% vs 79.5%) and severity compared with fentanyl-based PCA.

Perioperative IV dextrose administration may decrease postoperative nausea but not vomiting, based on a meta-analysis of 11 trials with 1,150 primarily women. In an earlier meta-analysis of 9 RCTs with 987 patients, perioperative IV dextrose was not associated with a significant reduction in postoperative nausea and vomiting.

One session of preoperative electroacupuncture was helpful for reducing the incidence of PONV by about 60% among 413 patients undergoing laparoscopic surgery and treated with multimodal antiemetic methods.

The 2023 guideline from the Multinational Association of Supportive Care in Cancer and the European Society for Medical Oncology classify chemotherapeutic drugs according to their emetogenic potential as high (intravenous agents cause emesis in >90% and oral agents in >30% of patients), moderate, low and minimal (intravenous agents’ risk of emesis in 10-30% or fewer and oral agents considered low/minimal risk if <30% risk) and offer recommendations based on this potential.
For both anthracycline-cyclophosphamide (AC) chemotherapy and non-AC chemotherapy of high emetic risk, they recommend a four-drug regimen including single doses of a 5-HT3 RA, dexamethasone, an NK1-RA (aprepitant, fosaprepitant, netupitant, fosnetupitant or rolapitant) and olanzapine given before chemotherapy. A Olanzapine on days 2-4 following AC regimens and dexamethasone-olanzapine on days 2-4 for non-AC regimens are recommended to prevent delayed nausea and vomiting. B For carboplatin-based moderate emetic risk chemotherapy in a dose of area under the concentration curve (mg) x 5 or more, they recommend a 3-drug regimen consisting of 5-HT3-RA, dexamethasone and an NK1-RA. SORT A For doses with AUC <5, there are no data justifying use of an NK1-RA. For additional recommendations, see the original document.

Among the 5-HT3 RAs used to prevent acute and delayed vomiting following highly emetogenic chemotherapy, ondansetron and granisetron appear to be equivalent. In a single trial, combination palonosetron and dexamethasone was superior to granisetron and dexamethasone in controlling delayed emesis.

Authors of a systematic review of 5 RCTs comparing palonosetron plus 1-day dexamethasone (d1 arm) vs. the same regimen followed by 2-3 days of dexamethasone (d3 arm) in chemotherapy-naive adult patients undergoing chemotherapy found no differences between groups in complete response rate.

Aprepitant added to a standard regimen of 5-HT3 RA and glucocorticoid significantly improved complete response in overall (OR 1.88, 95% CI 1.71 to 2.07), acute (OR 1.96, 95% CI 1.65 to 2.32) and delayed (OR 1.96, 95% CI 1.70 to 2.27) nausea and vomiting. Aprepitant was associated with decreased risk of constipation (OR 0.85, 95% CI 0.74 to 0.97) but increased incidence of hiccup (OR 1.26, 95% CI 1.05 to 1.51).

In an RCT of olanzapine, an atypical antipsychotic, vs. placebo, in combination with dexamethasone, aprepitant or fosaprepitant, and a 5-hydroxytryptamine type 3-receptor antagonist in patients receiving high-emetogenic chemotherapy, there were more patients in the olanzapine arm with no nausea during the overall 120-hour period (37% vs. 22%) but more sedation (severe in 5%) on day 2. Similarly, olanzapine vs. aprepitant added to combination dexamethasone and ondansetron resulted in less severe nausea following highly-emetic chemotherapy, although other outcome measures were similar.

In an RCT of 114 patients on chemotherapy for breast cancer, use of auricular acupuncture (both true and sham procedures) plus standard antiemetic treatment and care was superior to the use of standard antiemetic treatment alone in managing chemotherapy-induced nausea. Similarly, authors of a systematic review and meta-analysis of 14 papers found electrostimulation of acupuncture point Pericardium 6 reduced the mean number of episodes of acute nausea (mean difference [MD] -2.08; 95% CI -2.76, -1.39) and acute vomiting (MD -0.91; 95% CI -1.39, -0.42) in patients on chemotherapy.

Authors of a systematic review of 23 RCTs found no benefit of a ginger supplement vs. placebo or an antiemetic agent on chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting, although those taking more than 1 g of ginger supplementation daily for more than four days had significantly less acute vomiting than the control group (OR 0.3, 95% CI 0.12 to 0.8; I2 = 36%).
Opioid-induced nausea, vomiting and pruritus can be reduced with use of naloxone.

In an RCT of 121 children undergoing procedural sedation with intramuscular (IM) ketamine, those randomized to intramuscular ketamine plus 4 mg/kg ondansetron had reduced vomiting during recovery and before discharge compared with ketamine alone (12.5% vs. 21.5% and 1.8% vs. 9.2%, respectively).

In another RCT of 442 children undergoing procedural sedation with intranasal fentanyl and nitrous oxide, preoperative ondansetron given 30 to 60 minutes before nitrous oxide administration was not effective compared to placebo in preventing early vomiting (12% vs. 16%, respectively).

Medications suggested as prophylactic therapy for patients with moderate to severe CVS include tricyclic antidepressants (e.g., amitriptyline 25 mg at bedtime), anticonvulsants, aprepitant, and nutritional supplements (e.g., coenzyme Q, riboflavin).
Duration of symptoms, frequency, and severity are key to diagnosis. C
For patients with persistent or severe symptoms, order a CBC, basic metabolic profile, and pregnancy test (for adolescent and adult patients at risk for pregnancy). C

Often with diarrhea, onset 6-12 hours after ingestion, fever, cramping
Vomiting within 1 hour of meal ingestion, distension, hypo or hyperactive BS
Insidious, more than 1 hour after meal ingestion, partial digestion of food
Missed menstrual period in female of child bearing age, morning occurrences
Average length 6 days per episode, at least 3 episodes yearly, no vomiting between episodes
Right upper quadrant (RUQ) pain, positive Murphy's sign
Left upper quadrant (LUQ) pain, radiation to back, lipase elevation, large food or ethanol ingestion
Morning vomiting, projectile vomiting, absence of nausea, focal neurologic deficit
History of psych illness, habitual postprandial nausea and vomiting
Presence of vertigo, nystagmus, postural instability
Fever, palpable mass, fecal blood, tenderness, weight loss, jaundice
Elevation in troponin, ST elevation on ECG, chest pain
Watery diarrhea, fever, headache, abdominal cramping, lasting 1-10 days
Bloody diarrhea, WBCs in stool, positive stool culture, abdominal cramping
Repeated episodes of vomiting among daily long-term marijuana users, positive drug test

list.listitem: Obtain a detailed prescription and non-prescription medication list; consider medication side effect, especially if symptoms occurred in relationship to a new medication.

Duration of symptoms, frequency, and severity are key to diagnosis. Sudden onset suggests gastroenteritis, pancreatitis, cholecystitis, or drug-related effect. More insidious onset of nausea without vomiting suggests gastroparesis, pregnancy, metabolic disorders, or gastroesophageal reflux.

Assess characteristics of episodes. Projectile vomiting suggests intracranial disorders. Gastroparesis and gastric outlet obstruction tend to be delayed more than 1 hour after meal ingestion. Interestingly, patients younger than age 70 years with gastroparesis appear to have more nausea with vomiting and abdominal pain compared with older patients who report more early satiety and bloating based on the U.S. National Inpatient Sample database.
Most patients with CVS (65%) report prodromal symptoms including panic and a sense of doom lasting a median of 1 hour before the onset of vomiting (see below for Rome IV criteria).

In a retrospective chart review of 201 young patients admitted to a large children's health care system with either cannabinoid hyperemesis syndrome (CHS) or cyclic vomiting syndrome, those with CHS were older (mean age 18.1 vs. 14.5 years), more likely to have a positive urine drug screen (86% vs 2.9%) and had higher average systolic blood pressure (124.5 vs. 118.5 mm Hg). There were no significant differences in sex, race, ethnicity, or hospital length of stay between groups.

Quality and quantity of vomitus: Regurgitation of undigested food suggests esophageal disorders. Partially digested food infers gastroparesis or gastric outlet obstruction. Bilious vomit is characteristic of small bowel obstruction.

Associated symptoms: Presence of abdominal pain, diarrhea, or fever suggest infection or gastroenteritis. Pain preceding vomiting indicates an organic lesion, such as obstruction. Pain with small bowel obstruction may be temporarily relieved after vomiting. Presence of vertigo, photophobia, or focal neurological deficits suggests a central cause, such as brain tumor. Significant weight loss is associated with malignancy. Patients with CVS may report associated constitutional, cognitive, affective, autonomic and/or motor symptoms.

Physical examination: Assess for presence of jaundice, abdominal masses, lymphadenopathy, location of pain on palpation, and signs of dehydration. Auscultation of the abdomen may reveal high pitched, decreased or absent bowel sounds. Inspection of teeth or fingers may reveal loss of enamel or signs of self-induced vomiting.

Red flags for dehydration in children under age 5 years include appearing unwell or deteriorating, altered responsiveness (e.g., lethargic, irritable), sunken eyes, reduced skin turgor, tachycardia, and tachypnea.
Selection of diagnostic tests to evaluate the cause of nausea and vomiting should be based on the history and physical examination.
A CBC, basic metabolic profile, and pregnancy test (in adolescent and adult patients at risk of pregnancy) are recommended for patients with persistent or severe symptoms.
If suspected drug toxicity, obtain appropriate drug levels for salicylates, acetaminophen, digoxin, or suspected drug such as THC for cyclic vomiting.
Obtain serum lipase for suspected pancreatitis and an abdominal ultrasound for suspected cholecystitis.
Consider abdominal CT with oral and IV contrast or abdominal radiographs for suspected bowel obstruction, pancreatic cancer or other malignancy, or appendicitis.
Obtain stool culture for suspected bacterial gastroenteritis and diarrhea (acute).
Consider gastric emptying scintigraphy for suspected gastroparesis delayed gastric emptying.
Obtain Helicobacter pylori antibody for suspected non ulcer dyspepsia.
Obtain ECG and troponin I for suspected myocardial infarction.
Consider RUQ ultrasound for abnormal liver function test evaluation.

The American Gastroenterological Association (AGA) guidelines for CVS recommend a basic workup including blood work (ie, complete blood count, serum electrolytes and glucose, liver function testing, and lipase), urinalysis, and a one-time esophagogastroduodenoscopy or other mode of upper gastrointestinal imaging to exclude obstructive lesions.
Evaluate for complications of nausea and vomiting including volume depletion, malnutrition, electrolyte imbalance, and vitamin deficiencies.

Relevant clinical decision rules include a decision rule to diagnose bowel obstruction and the Alvarado (MANTRELS) score for appendicitis. The symptom of abdominal pain before vomiting was useful for ruling out appendicitis in one study with a sensitivity of 96% and specificity of 17%; this item added an additional 12% (increased from 32% to 44%) when combined with the Alvarado score, without any false negatives.
A validated score can be used to predict the likelihood of PONV.

Rome IV diagnostic criteria for CVS are: Stereotypical episodes of acute-onset vomiting lasting <7 days; at least 3 discrete episodes in a year, 2 of which have occurred in the prior 6 months; episodes should be separated by at least 1 week of baseline health; absence of vomiting between episodes; milder symptoms such as nausea, occasional vomiting, and dyspepsia may be present.
See algorithm in for a suggested approach to the patient who presents with nausea and vomiting.
Antiemetic drugs (e.g., ondansetron, dexamethasone, droperidol) are useful in treating nausea and vomiting in pregnancy, PONV, and nausea and vomiting in children with gastroenteritis. A
Alternative methods, including use of ginger and acupressure of all types, have been shown to reduce PONV and nausea in pregnancy. A

A number of antiemetic drugs, including ondansetron, dexamethasone, droperidol, are useful in treating nausea and vomiting in pregnancy, PONV, and nausea and vomiting in children with gastroenteritis.

In one study of 97 patients with severe nausea, droperidol 1.25 mg was more effective in reducing nausea than 10 mg of metoclopramide or 10 mg of prochlorperazine, or placebo. However, more patients taking droperidol experienced akathisia by 24 hours (71% vs. 23% with all other medications).

Authors of a Cochrane review of drugs for PONV identified 8 drugs as useful: droperidol, metoclopramide, ondansetron, tropisetron, dolasetron, dexamethasone, cyclizine and granisetron. Differences between drugs were not found given the limited evidence. In addition, the authors note that only 10 of every 100 drug-treated patients would likely benefit and 1 to 5 per 100 would experience a mild side effect such as headache from drug treatment. For patients who fail preventive PONV treatment, consider use of a rescue antiemetic from a different drug class.

In a meta-analysis of 120 studies in patients with PONV, including 27,787 patients, the least safe drug combination was granisetron and dexamethasone which was associated with a significantly higher risk of arrhythmia. In this study, authors found that the safest approach was to use either ondansetron plus dexamethasone, or dolasetron. They also found little difference with respect to safety between the individual drugs including ramosetron, granisetron, ondansetron, tropisetron, and dolasetron.

Among the 5-HT3 RAs used to prevent acute and delayed vomiting following highly-emetogenic chemotherapy, ondansetron and granisetron appear to be equivalent. In a single trial, combination palonosetron and dexamethasone was superior to granisetron and dexamethasone in controlling delayed emesis.

The NK1-RA rolapitant appears to be safe and effective in controlling chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting in patients receiving moderately and highly emetogenic chemotherapy. Rolapitant has a longer half-life (180 h) than other similar agents and does not induce or inhibit CYP34A, which may be an advantage of this drug

Authors of a meta-analysis found a modest benefit of cannabinoids on nausea and vomiting from chemotherapy (NNT 3-7). Adverse effects included feeling high, disorientation, and confusion (number needed to treat to harm [NNTH] = 2-15).
Among palliative care patients, there is insufficient evidence to support use of haloperidol or droperidol to control nausea and vomiting.
Treatment options include antiemetics (aprepitant), prokinetics (prucalopride, relamorelin) and fundic relaxants (acotiamide, buspirone).

Authors of a systematic review of 24 RCTs on diabetic gastroparesis found metoclopramide to be the only approved and effective drug for accelerating gastric emptying and improving symptoms. Adverse effects of metoclopramide include cardiovascular and nervous systems which might be resolved with a new intranasal preparation. Alternatives are oral domperidone for patients without cardiovascular risk factors, intravenous erythromycin for hospitalized patients, and possibly relamorelin and prucalopride.

Authors of a more recent systematic review found that although metoclopramide had benefit on nausea and bloating, based on weak evidence, it was not effective overall. There was benefit on global symptom scores to a greater extent than placebo for clebopride (Clanzoflat, Cleboril), a dopamine antagonist and chemical cousin to metoclopramide, and domperidone. However, clebopride is not widely available and domperidone is not available in the United States, except as an investigational drug.
Cyclic Vomiting Syndrome (CVS)

Recommended abortive medications for patients with moderate to severe CVS include triptans (sumatriptan 20 mg intranasally or 6 mg subcutaneously), antiemetics (e.g., ondansetron, promethazine, prochlorperazine), and sedatives (e.g., lorazepam).

listitem.strong: Alcohol use disorder (AUD), and cannabinoid hyperemesis syndrome (CHS)

list.listitem: The Academic Emergency Medicine (SAEM) Guidelines for adult patients with AUD or CHS presenting to the emergency department suggest the following:
Patients with moderate to severe alcohol withdrawal who are being admitted to hospital: phenobarbital in addition to benzodiazepines alone (low to very low certainty of evidence).

Patients with AUD who desire alcohol cessation: prescription for one anti-craving medication (very low certainty of evidence) and naltrexone to prevent return to heavy drinking (low certainty of evidence). If naltrexone is contraindicated, consider acamprosate (low certainty of evidence). Gabapentin can also be used to reduce heavy drinking days and improve alcohol withdrawal symptoms (very low certainty of evidence).

Patients with CHS: haloperidol or droperidol (in addition to usual care/serotonin antagonists, e.g., ondansetron) to help with symptom management (very low certainty of evidence) and offering use of topical capsaicin (in addition to usual care/serotonin antagonists, e.g., ondansetron) to help with symptom management (very low certainty of evidence).

Authors of a systematic review of five observational studies and two RCTs including 492 patients with CHS found clinical benefit for the 2 studies of dopamine antagonists compared to usual care or no active comparator and mixed evidence for the efficacy of capsaicin for reducing nausea and emesis.
In an emergency department study of 115 adults presenting with NV, inhalation of isopropyl alcohol reduced nausea within several minutes compared to placebo.

Options for refractory gastroparesis include gastric peroral endoscopic myotomy, found clinically successful in 75.8% (95% CI 68.1 to 82.1) in one case series, surgical pyloroplasty with a similar success rate, and gastric electric stimulation with or without pyloroplasty.
Pyloric injections of botulinum toxin A provided symptomatic improvement at 1 month in 64% of 25 of 34 patients with refractory gastroparesis who were available for follow-up.

Ginger, in a number of different oral forms, reduced the incidence of acute chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting, RR 0.60, 95% CI 0.42. to 0.86, in one meta-analysis of 10 studies. This finding was confirmed in another meta-analysis of 3 RCTs with an OR compared to control groups of 0.4, 95% CI 0.17 to 0.81.
In a study of home remedies for digestive symptoms, coke was used by 10% of 1012 subjects surveyed and reported as effective for nausea or vomiting by 89.6%.

Cannabinoids, in particular dronabinol and nabilone vs. an active comparator, improved nausea and vomiting (SMD -0.28; 95%CI -0.47 to -0.1 and -0.44; 95%CI -0/62 to -0.26, respectively) when used for that indication, but the difference did not reach significance compared to placebo.
Peppermint oil applied between the upper lip and nose three-times daily for 5 days following chemotherapy reduced the severity of N and frequency of N and V in a quasi-RCT in Turkey.

Acupuncture-point stimulation of any type (needles, electrical, acupressure, magnetic) reduced incidence of acute chemotherapy-induced vomiting. Acupuncture did not reduce nausea severity. Conversely, acupressure reduced mean acute nausea severity but not acute vomiting.

According to a 2025 Cochrane network meta-analysis including 77 RCTs and 9847 participants, stimulation of P6 acupoint(s) on the wrist and antiemetics technique of patients undergoing surgery combined with antiemetrics reduces the risk of PONV compared to sham treatment.
Transcutaneous electrical acupoint stimulation was also effective for preventing PONV with a RR of 0.54, 95% CI 0.42 to 0.68 based on a meta-analysis of 14 RCTs.

With respect to aromatherapy for PONV, Cochrane authors concluded that aromatherapy was no more effective than placebo for nausea severity, but patients on aromatherapy, including isopropyl alcohol, were less likely to require rescue antiemetics; quality of evidence was low.
In one RCT of 206 patients undergoing laparoscopic cholecystectomy, traditional dry cupping delivered in the operation room reduced PONV severity compared to sham treatment.

There is some supporting evidence for guided imagery, behavioral therapy, and relaxation therapy for GI symptoms. Music therapy may be helpful for reducing the incidence of anticipatory chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting and lowering the severity of delayed vomiting.

Authors of a systematic review of nonpharmacologic nursing interventions to reduce or prevent PONV found effective interventions included acupuncture, aromatherapy, oral intake of ginger, listening to music, education, and visits to patients.
Suggestive interventions such as hypnosis reduce postoperative anxiety and pain intensity, but do not appear effective in reducing nausea or postoperative analgesic drug consumption.

Early postoperative feeding after major abdominal gynecologic surgery appears safe without increasing nausea, vomiting, abdominal distention or other postoperative complications. Recovery of bowel function is faster with early feeding.
Nausea in pregnancy can begin in the first week of conception and last beyond 22 weeks’ gestation. B
Nausea and vomiting related to food poisoning usually resolves in 24 to 28 hours. C
Nausea and vomiting in viral gastroenteritis can last up to 10 days. C

In an observational study of 39 patients with CHS, most reported persistent CHS symptoms including abdominal pain, nausea, or cyclic vomiting in the 2-week period following an emergency department (ED) visit with a median duration of 7 days. Most participants returned to prior cannabis use patterns within a few days and 25% of participants who completed 3-month follow-up reported recurrent ED visits for cyclic vomiting.

The presence of gastrointestinal symptoms is not associated with higher mortality in patients with COVID-19, but children with diarrhea and COVID-19 (not NV) appear to have a more severe clinical course (pooled OR 3.97; 95% CI 1.80-8.73). Prolonged nausea was present in 3.23% (95% CI 0.54%-16.53%) of 527 COVID-19 survivors and vomiting persisted in 3.19% 995% CI 1.62%-6.17%) of 2,238 COVID-19 survivors based on a systematic review and meta-analysis.

In a prospective study of 195 pregnant women, a total of 74% of women reported nausea, as early as the first week of conception. The mean gestational age of onset was 6 weeks, and nausea lasted a mean of 35 days. A total of 51% of subjects reported vomiting, which began as early as 4 weeks gestation. The peak time of nausea and vomiting severity occurred at 11 to 13 weeks. Although 50% of women with nausea reported that it resolved by 14 weeks, it took until 22 weeks for nausea to resolve in 90% of the women.
About 3% of women experience hyperemesis gravidarum (see Hyperemesis Gravidarum).

The Royal College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists published their 2024 guidelines on nausea and vomiting in pregnancy and hyperemesis gravidarum. The guidelines recommend use of a validated index of nausea and vomiting such as the Pregnancy-Unique Quantification of Emesis or HyperEmesis Level Prediction tool to classify the severity of nausea and vomiting of pregnancy and hyperemesis (Grade C), noting that ketonuria should not be used as an indicator of dehydration or severity. They recommend anti (H1) histamines, phenothiazines and doxylamine/pyridoxine (Xonvea®) as first-line agents. Ondansetron is recommended as a second-line agent based on the small increase in the absolute risk of orofacial clefting with ondansetron use in the first trimester which may be offset by the risk associated with poorly managed hyperemesis.

Antiemetic medication appears to reduce the frequency of nausea in pregnancy. Drugs used in multiple trials included antihistamines, vitamin B6, Debendox (Bendectin), and ginger. Authors of a systematic review of nausea and vomiting in pregnancy found benefit greater than placebo for ginger, pyridoxine, antihistamines, metoclopramide, and ondansetron for mild symptoms and pyridoxine-doxylamine, promethazine, metoclopramide, and ondansetron for moderate symptoms. Corticosteroids may be useful in severe cases.
In a recent RCT of 36 pregnant women, ondansetron was more effective than a pyridoxine/doxylamine combination for reducing nausea and vomiting in early pregnancy with a NNT of about 2.

In a population study from Denmark, ondansetron used to treat nausea and vomiting during pregnancy (vs. non-exposed women) was not associated with a significantly increased risk of spontaneous abortion, stillbirth, major birth defects, preterm delivery, delivery of a low-birth-weight infant, or delivery of a small-for-gestational-age infant.

Other interventions assessed include acupressure, acustimulation, acupuncture, chamomile, lemon oil and mint oil. Authors of a Cochrane review found a lack of high-quality evidence to support any particular intervention, including drugs listed above. There was limited support for P6 acupressure, auricular acupressure and acustimulation of the P6 point, but not for acupuncture. Evidence was also limited, but overall positive for vitamin B6, anti-emetic drugs, and ginger.

For nausea and vomiting in pregnancy, ginger in the form of powered ginger root capsules (250 mg before meals and at bedtime) was helpful in reducing both nausea (lower scores on a nausea scale) and vomiting (1.3-1.5 fewer episodes a day).

Authors of a systematic review of alternative medicine treatments found matricaria chamomilla, elettaria cardamomum, pomegranate and spearmint syrup, lemon and ginger helpful for reducing pregnancy-associated nausea and vomiting.

For PONV, authors of a meta-analysis of 10 studies with 979 children concluded that compared to placebo or benzodiazepine, clonidine 4 μg/kg premedication reduced PONV as well as post-operative pain in children undergoing ophthalmic surgery without evidence of major hemodynamic instability.

For children undergoing emetogenic chemotherapy, 5-HT3 RAs appear effective for prevention of vomiting; fewer trials reported on nausea. Granisetron or palonosetron are possibly better than ondansetron. Adding dexamethasone improves control of vomiting, although the risk-benefit profile of adding steroid is uncertain.

The Pediatric Oncology Group of Ontario 2022 guideline recommends use of three drugs (5-HT3 RA+dexamethasone+aprepitant) to prevent acute phase chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting or palonosetron+aprepitant in patients unable to receive dexamethasone. Palonosetron is the preferred 5HT3 RA in patients at high risk of delayed phase chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting. A table of medications, their strength of recommendation, and dosages is available in the cited paper.

For evaluation of bilious vomiting in a neonate up to 1 week old, the American College of Radiology recommends an initial abdomen x-ray followed by an upper GI series if indicated; an upper GI series is suggested for bilious vomiting in the 1 week to 3 month old infant. For projectile vomiting in infants up to 3 months, an abdominal ultrasound is recommended (acr.org).

For children under age 5 years without dehydration treated at home, NICE recommends continued usual feeds and encouraging fluids (fruit juices and carbonated drinks should not be encouraged) and offering oral rehydration (ORS) solution if at risk for dehydration. For children with clinical dehydration, use ORS solution at 50 ml/kg for rehydration plus maintenance volume over a 4-hour period in small amounts at a time, continue breastfeeding as well if applicable and avoid solid fluids until rehydrated and then advance as tolerated.

Ondansetron is effective for use in children with gastroenteritis, resulting in reduced vomiting when given liquids (14% vs. 35%; NNT 5), fewer vomiting episodes (0.18 vs. 0.65) and less need for IV hydration (14% vs. 31%; NNT 5). Doses were 2 mg in children 8 to 15 kg, 4 mg in children 15 to 30 kg, and 8 mg for those weighing more than 30 kg.

This was confirmed in a recent RCT with 194 children with gastroenteritis in which ondansetron at 0.1 mg/kg compared to oral rehydration fluid alone decreased the proportion of children who continued vomiting within 4 hours (42.9% vs. 19.5%, OR 0.37; 95% CI 0.20 to 0.72, NNT=4), significantly decreased the number of vomiting episodes within 4 hours and improved overall parental satisfaction with treatment.

In a RCT involving 1013 children aged 6 months to 18 years who presented to the emergency department with no more than 3 days of gastroenteritis and at least 3 episodes of vomiting in the previous 24 hours, ondansetron (0.15 mg/kg, up to 8 mg) reduced the likelihood of developing moderate to severe gastroenteritis after discharge.
Metoclopramide is also superior to placebo in reducing vomiting due to gastroenteritis in children.

Conversely, in children who experienced vomiting after initial oral rehydration in the emergency department, there was no statistically significant difference in the proportion of patients with vomiting at 24 hours randomized to granisetron vs. placebo.

In a 7-year retrospective case series, use of ondansetron in children with a negative head CT following head injury (used in 3.7% of children in 2003 and 22% of children in 2010) was associated with a lower likelihood of returning to the ED within 72 hours after controlling for demographic and acuity differences.
Cannabinoids appear to be effective in managing chemotherapy-related nausea and vomiting in children, but studies are generally of poor quality.
